title: Death to the Spreadsheet: Why I Finally Ditched QLA
author: Joel Kenyon
summary: Joel Kenyon explains why he abandoned Question Level Analysis (QLA) spreadsheets in his science department after over a decade of them being treated as the gold standard of data-driven teaching. Working through concrete GCSE Biology examples, he shows that QLA's core assumption -- that all questions on a topic are equivalent and that closing a gap on one question closes the underlying knowledge gap -- is false: two questions both nominally 'about valves' can test entirely different knowledge, guessability, and mark weighting, so plugging a gap for one specific question tells you little about whether students will succeed on a differently-phrased question next time. He also dismantles the myth that exam boards guarantee balanced curriculum coverage within five years (calling belief in predictable question cycles a textbook Gambler's Fallacy), and argues that re-teaching a QLA-flagged 'gap' produces only a temporary performance bump that confuses performance with durable learning, given the forgetting curve. Kenyon's alternative is unglamorous: because well-run formative assessment (mini-whiteboards, Do Nows, live questioning) already surfaces the gaps a teacher needs to know, QLA mostly just re-confirms information teachers already have at the cost of substantial data-entry time that could go toward planning better intervention.
points: Central claim: QLA falsely assumes all questions on a 'topic' are interchangeable, when mark value, guessability, and what's actually being assessed vary enormously between similarly-labelled questions -- making gap-plugging based on QLA unreliable.

Names the belief that exam boards must cover the full specification within five years as a Gambler's Fallacy, arguing there's no formal obligation to rotate topics predictably and that trying to 'predict the paper' is a fool's errand exam boards actively guard against.

Distinguishes performance from learning: a post-intervention 80% success rate on re-tested questions reflects a short-term bump, not evidence the knowledge has survived the forgetting curve three weeks later.

Documents a concrete failure mode where re-teaching a QLA-flagged Biology gap improves the next mock's Biology score while Chemistry silently degrades -- the recency effect masquerading as genuine gap-closure.

Argues that because good formative assessment already reveals gaps in real time, QLA data entry (often 30+ minutes per assessment plus duplicate uploads to a central system) mostly just rubber-stamps what teachers already knew, at high time cost.
quotes: [1] "For over a decade, QLAs have been championed as the pinnacle of data-driven teaching. They generate a mountain of statistics on how a student performed on X or Y. However, there is a catch: QLAs often fail to identify the actual root of the problem.

[2] "But…have these gaps actually been closed, or have we simply achieved a temporary bump in performance? We often mistake performance for learning. If we re-tested those same students three weeks later without the guided feedback session fresh in their minds, would that 80% still hold up?

[3] "The fundamental flaw in relying on QLA is the assumption that all questions are created equal. In reality, a topic is not a monolith, and the way a question is phrased can completely change what the data actually tells you.

[4] "There is an often quoted myth that exam boards must assess everything in the paper within a 5-year period. This is not true... Believing that 'alveoli haven't been tested in three years, so they're due this summer' is a classic demonstration of the Gambler's Fallacy.

[5] "They performed better on Biology is because you have literally just covered it. They performed worse on Chemistry because it has been weeks, if not months, since you have revised this content. It is a prime demonstration of the forgetting curve.

[6] "Formalising this with an assessment and a QLA does absolutely nothing but rubber stamp what I already knew... If I was to wait until my QLA document was filled in, it could be 2 months before I go over it again. This is a waste of time.

[7] "Ultimately, QLA prioritises the administration of data over actual teaching. It treats assessments as exhaustive when they are merely samples, and it ignores the fact that a student's success on a feedback task doesn't guarantee they have retained that knowledge for the long term.
